children.translated_text: Homage to <s>Indirā</s>, whose greatness is immeasurable, who gives joy to practitioners, who grants every prosperity and accomplishment, and who destroys the darkness of misfortune;
who was born from the ocean of nectar, whose own form is golden, and who is the wife of the enemy of <s>Madhu</s>.

children.text: dhyātvā saṃprati gauraveṇa caraṇadvandvaṃ śubhaṃ gauravaṃ śrībrahmānvitaśaṅkareṇa sahasā vaidyapriyānāmikā
children.translated_text: Having now reverently meditated on the auspicious pair of feet, this graceful vernacular exposition on the examination of the pulse, called dear to physicians and connected with venerable <s>Brahmā</s> and <s>Śaṅkara</s>,

children.text: vyākhyā śrījayakṛṣṇadāsakathanānnāḍīparīkṣopari prītyai sadbhiṣajāṃ vidhīyata iyaṃ bhāṣāmayī śobhanā
children.translated_text: is composed for the pleasure of good physicians, from the teaching of <s>Śrījayakṛṣṇadāsa</s>.
One should examine eight places of the body of one afflicted by disease:
the <s>nāḍī</s> (pulse), urine, feces, tongue, sound, touch, sight, and bodily appearance.

children.text: rugṇasya mugdhasya vimohitasya dīpaḥ padārthāniva jīvanāḍī
children.translated_text: For a sick, confused, or deluded person, the life-pulse is like a lamp revealing objects;
it shows the form produced by the <s>doṣas</s> (humoral faults), whether separate, combined, or joined in pairs.
There is a certain pulse situated within the pulse that runs in the forearm;
that is called the life-pulse by <s>Nandin</s>, knower of reality.
It is especially to be examined at the base of the thumb;

children.text: sā hi sarvāṅgagā nāḍī pūrvācāryaiḥ subhāṣitā ||
children.translated_text: for the ancient teachers have well said that this pulse pervades all the limbs.
Leaving one finger's breadth below from the base of the thumb,
the careful physician should examine it; it is perceived only through practice.
The artery at the region of the base of the thumb is witness to life;

children.text: tacceṣṭayā sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ jñeyaṃ kāyasya paṇḍitaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: by its activity, the wise should know the ease and suffering of the body.
For women, the physician should carefully know the pulse in the left hand and left foot;
for men, especially on the right side.
On the foot, it is below the ankle, in the region of the big toe, from the base of the big toe.
Leaving one finger's breadth, one should examine it at the wrist,
pressing downward with the hand again and again by means of three fingers.
With the left hand gently supporting the patient's elbow,
the excellent physician should carefully examine the throbbing of the pulse
according to scripture, his own experience, or the transmitted tradition.

children.text: ādau vātavahā nāḍī madhye vahati pittalā
children.translated_text: At first the vāta-bearing pulse flows; in the middle the pitta pulse flows;
at the end, with the disorder of phlegm, the pulse is regarded as threefold.
When vāta is excessive, the pulse is clearly manifest beneath the index finger;
in pitta it is manifest beneath the middle finger, and in kapha it goes to the third finger.
When vāta and pitta are excessive, it is distinct between the index and middle fingers;
when vāta and kapha are present, it is manifest between the index and ring fingers.
When pitta and kapha are present, it is distinct between the middle and ring fingers;
from a sannipāta, a disorder of all three, it is very manifest under all three fingers.
In vāta the pulse has a crooked movement; the pitta-bearing pulse is restless.

children.text: sthirā śleṣmavatī proktā sarvaliṅgā ca sarvagā
children.translated_text: The phlegmatic pulse is said to be steady, while the pulse of all signs goes everywhere.

children.text: śleṣmaṇā stimitā stabdhā miśrāṃ miśraistu lakṣayet ||
children.translated_text: With phlegm it is sluggish and fixed; one should recognize mixed pulses from mixed causes.
When vāta is predominant it makes a movement like that of a leech or a snake;
when pitta is predominant, that pulse has the movement of a crow or a frog;
when kapha is predominant, it moves like a goose, or like a pigeon.

children.text: nāḍī dhatte tridoṣe tu gatiṃ tittiralāvayoḥ
children.translated_text: When all three <s>doṣas</s> are present, the pulse takes on the movement of a partridge or a quail;
sometimes the pulse goes slowly, and sometimes it moves rapidly.
In a disease arising from two <s>doṣas</s>, physicians should recognize it in this way.
Sometimes it flows slow, sometimes sharp, and sometimes broken;
sometimes subtle, sometimes gross: such is the movement of the pulse in an incurable disease.
If the pulse is seen above the skin and flows very restlessly,
it is said to be a sign of incurability, being slimy and very restless.
If, connected upward from the thumb, it flows evenly,
that pulse should be known by experts in pulse-signs as free from fault.

children.text: sthitvā sthitvā vahati yā sā nāḍī mṛtyudāyinī
children.translated_text: The pulse that flows stopping and starting is death-giving;

children.text: atiśītā ca yā nāḍī rogiṇaḥ prāṇahāriṇī ||
children.translated_text: a pulse that is extremely cold takes away the life of the patient.
A hot and rapid pulse arises when fever is aggravated,
and likewise in agitation, anger, desire, and the arising of fear or anxiety.
A pulse of diminished movement should be recognized by the best physicians;
in one whose bodily constituents are depleted and whose digestive fire is weak, it certainly becomes still slower.

children.text: gurvī soṣṇā ca raktena pūrṇā nāḍī prajāyate
children.translated_text: From blood there arises a heavy, somewhat hot, and full pulse;
a pulse with <s>āma</s> (undigested matter) is heavy, and it is also slow and filled with blood.
In one with blazing digestive fire it flows lightly, and it is also regarded as rapid.
For one who is comfortable, the pulse is steady and strong.

children.text: capalā kṣudhitasya syātsthirā tṛptasya sā bhavet
children.translated_text: It is restless in one who is hungry, and steady in one who is satisfied;

children.text: sthirā śleṣmavatī nāḍī vahati pradare tathā ||
children.translated_text: a steady, phlegmatic pulse also flows in pradarā.

children.text: ajīrṇe tu bhavennāḍī kaṭhinā parito jaḍā
children.translated_text: In indigestion the pulse is hard and dull all around;

children.text: capalā rasaje dīrghā pitte vegavatī tathā ||
children.translated_text: it is restless in a disorder of rasa, long, and in pitta it is rapid.

children.text: prasannā ca drutā śīghrā kṣudbhir nāḍī pravartate
children.translated_text: When there is hunger, the pulse proceeds clear, swift, and quick;

children.text: jvare tīvrā prasannā ca nāḍī vahati pittataḥ ||
children.translated_text: in fever, from pitta, the pulse flows sharp and clear.
In rasa it is said to be oily and full of fluid, producing fainting.
Pulse examination is performed in a healthy person in order to awaken knowledge of future disease.
The pulse that arises from burden, blows, fainting, fear, grief, or cholera-like illness,

children.text: saṃmūrchitāpi gāḍhaṃ punarapi sā jīvitaṃ bhajate ||
children.translated_text: although deeply stunned, nevertheless again attains life.

children.text: mehe'rśasi malājīrṇe śīghraṃ tu spandate dharā ||
children.translated_text: In urinary disease, piles, fecal disorder, and indigestion, the pulse quickly throbs in the earth-element manner.

children.text: gurvīṃ vātavahāṃ nāḍīṃ garbheṇa saha lakṣayet
children.translated_text: Together with pregnancy, one should identify a heavy vāta-bearing pulse.
There the conditions of pitta and vāyu are to be described by lightness and heaviness.
The distinction between unripe and ripe, and the reckoning of days, months, and so on, is made by the wise.

children.text: saiva pittavahā laghvī naṣṭagarbhā vadecca tām ||
children.translated_text: That same light pitta-bearing pulse would indicate a lost pregnancy.
And in pain of the arm, crookedness, a blow, and trembling from fright...
During exercise and loud laughter the earth-bearing pulse does not attain throbbing.
The pulse that is deep should be the flesh-bearing one.

children.text: dīrghā kṛśā vātagatir viṣamā vepate dharā
children.translated_text: Long and thin is the movement of <s>vāta</s>; irregular, the earth-bearing pulse trembles.
It is life-destroying, confused by bad-smelling signs and by an accumulation of indigestion.
For one afflicted by cold, whose limbs are moist, it becomes subtle after a long time and then sluggish.
In one lying down and endowed with strength, the pulse obtains throbbing.
Having a slightly bent movement, it flows in its own place in the current.

children.text: sūkṣmarūpā sphuṭā śītā svasthānasthe kaphe tathā
children.translated_text: When <s>kapha</s> remains in its own place, it is subtle in form, clear, and cold.
Likewise, when <s>pitta</s> remains in its own place, it is strong, straight, and mobile.
It is not straight from an aggravation of <s>vāta</s>, and fierce from an aggravation of <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: saralā śleṣmakopena nāḍī doṣaiḥ pṛthak smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: From an aggravation of phlegm it is straight; the pulse is remembered separately according to the <s>doṣas</s>.
When <s>kapha</s> is deficient, the pulse carries an increased movement of <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: hīne vāte kaphe cāti svalpe pitte cirātsphuṭā ||
children.translated_text: When <s>vāta</s> is deficient and <s>kapha</s> is very slight, while <s>pitta</s> is slight, it becomes clear after a long time.

children.text: saumyā sūkṣmā sthirā mandā nāḍī sahajavātajā
children.translated_text: A gentle, subtle, steady, and slow pulse is born of innate <s>vāta</s>.
One that is slightly restless, crooked, and hard is born of <s>vāta</s> and <s>pitta</s>.

children.text: sthūlā ca cañcalā śītā mandā syācchleṣmavātajā
children.translated_text: One that is thick, restless, cold, and slow is born of <s>śleṣman</s> and <s>vāta</s>.
A subtle, cold, and steady pulse arises from <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
When <s>pitta</s> is excessive, and from eating pungent and similar foods, it becomes restless.
One who continually eats rough, dry food consumes what is <s>vātala</s>, vāta-producing.
For him the pulse, dominated by <s>vāta</s>, is dry and like a lump.
The pulse produced by the phlegmatic <s>doṣa</s> is thread-like, slow, and cold.
In one desirous of sex, in one whose passion has gone, and even in one walking, it behaves as in <s>vāta</s>.
In a child whose urges are obstructed, or in one pierced by a foreign body, it behaves as in <s>pitta</s>.
In one sleepy, fat, satisfied, or proud, it behaves as in <s>kapha</s>.
In indigestion from fecal matter it is declared to be even, subtle, and of minute pulsation.
From remaining fecal matter it is declared to be irregular, hard, and thick.

children.text: raktād ajīrṇādvamanād virekād vīryakṣayād raktasṛter nibandhāt
children.translated_text: From blood, indigestion, vomiting, purgation, loss of semen, bleeding, or obstruction,
and from fainting and the like, because of weakness of the digestive fire, the creature's pulse flows moving like a thread.
When free of <s>āma</s>, it should be known as subtle-moving; when filled with <s>kapha</s>,
the pulse is thread-like, slow, and cold, produced by the cold <s>doṣa</s>.
With moderate diet, joined with <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>, it moves very slowly.
In blood that produces much burning, it especially seems to flood.

children.text: madhye kare vahennāḍī yadi dīrghā punardrutā
children.translated_text: If the pulse flows in the middle of the hand, long and again swift,
then certainly the impurities in the person are filled with blood.

children.text: vakrā ca capalā śītasparśā vātajvare bhavet
children.translated_text: In a <s>vāta</s> fever it is crooked, restless, and cold to the touch.

children.text: drutā ca saralā dīrghā śīghrā pittajvare bhavet ||
children.translated_text: In a <s>pitta</s> fever it is swift, straight, long, and quick.

children.text: mandā ca susthirā śītā picchilā śleṣmake bhavet
children.translated_text: In a phlegmatic fever it is slow, very steady, cold, and slimy.
In a <s>pitta</s> fever the pulse flows long and straight like a lotus-fiber.
It carries itself quickly and not sluggishly; this is declared to arise from indigestion of wastes.

children.text: sthūlā ca kaṭhinā śīghraṃ spandate tīvramārute ||
children.translated_text: When the wind is intense, it is thick and hard and throbs quickly.

children.text: purā mandā ca śanakaiścaṇḍatāṃ yāti nāḍikā
children.translated_text: At first the pulse is slow, and then gradually it becomes fierce.

children.text: jvaraṃ śaityaṃ vepathorvā sambandhaṃ vrajati drutam ||
children.translated_text: It quickly comes into association with fever, coldness, or trembling.
This is considered the producer of one-day and similar diseases.
In seizure by spirits the vein is to be observed in a future one-day fever.
Sometimes it moves slowly, and sometimes it carries speed.
It should be known from the aggravation of two <s>doṣas</s>; displaced from its place, it kills.

children.text: raktapitte vahennāḍī mandā ca kaṭhinā ṛjuḥ
children.translated_text: In <s>raktapitta</s>, bleeding disorder, the pulse flows slow, hard, and straight.
In a phlegmatic cough it is steady and slow; in dyspnea its movement is intense.
In the king of diseases, the pulse is declared to have the gait of a snake.

children.text: madātyaye ca sūkṣmā syātkaṭhinā parito jaḍā ||
children.translated_text: In intoxication it is subtle, hard all around, and dull.
In piles the pulse is steady and slow, sometimes crooked and sometimes straight.
But in diarrhea it is slow, like a leech in the cold season.
In an increase of flesh, it takes on the movement seen in fever and diarrhea.
A pulse like a dead snake indicates <s>grahaṇī</s> disease.
In urinary obstruction, with repeated breaking and throbbing, it is flooded.

children.text: pramehe ca jaḍā sūkṣmā muhurāpyāyate sirā ||
children.translated_text: In <s>prameha</s> the vein is dull and subtle, and repeatedly swells up.
In <s>pāṇḍu</s> disease it is mobile and sharp, moving visibly and invisibly.

children.text: kuṣṭhe tu kaṭhinā nāḍī sthirā syād apravṛttikā ||
children.translated_text: In skin disease the pulse is hard, steady, and inactive.
In a <s>vāta</s> disease it is steady; when obstructed, it has all the signs.
In <s>balāsa</s> it is accompanied by throbbing, subtle, and rapid in movement.
In disorders above the clavicle, and according to the strength of the <s>doṣas</s>,
having understood their signs, the physician should state the earth-bearing movement.
Hard like the sun and moon and warm, that patient is dependent on blood.
The pulse of <s>sannipāta</s>, the conjunction of all three <s>doṣas</s>, is clear in movement by cold and heat.
Very thin and very swift, it subsides in <s>sannipāta</s>.
Cold and moving with an unctuous speed, it is fatal for that patient.

children.text: sthitvā sthitvā calantī yā sā smṛtā prāṇanāśinī
children.translated_text: The pulse that moves after stopping again and again is remembered as destroyer of life.

children.text: atitīkṣṇā ca śītā ca jīvitaṃ hantyasaṃśayam ||
children.translated_text: If it is extremely sharp and cold, it undoubtedly destroys life.
If the pulse is swift at the end of delirious speech, and at midday the fever is like fire,

children.text: dinaikaṃ jīvitaṃ tasya dvitīye maraṇaṃ dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: his life lasts one day; on the second day death is certain.
At the time of death the pulse becomes worn out, like a little drum.
Above, it is slow like a thread, but below it has become crooked.

children.text: yātyuccakāsthirā yā ca yā ceyaṃ māṃsavāhinī
children.translated_text: The pulse that goes high and unsteady, and this flesh-bearing pulse,

children.text: yātisūkṣmā ca vakrā ca tāmasādhyāṃ vinirdiśet ||
children.translated_text: and the one that goes very subtle and crooked: these indicate an incurable condition.
For the man whose pulse is steady at the mouth and is seen like the flash of lightning,

children.text: dinaikaṃ jīvitaṃ tasya dvitīye maraṇaṃ dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: his life lasts one day; on the second day death is certain.

children.text: mandaṃ mandaṃ kuṭilakuṭilaṃ vyākulaṃ vyākulaṃ vā sthitvā sthitvā vahati dhamanī yāti nāśaṃ ca sūkṣmā
children.translated_text: Slowly, slowly, crookedly, crookedly, or confusedly, confusedly, the subtle artery flows, stopping again and again, and goes toward destruction.

children.text: nityasthānātskhalati punarapyaṅguliṃ saṃspṛśetsā bhāvairevaṃ bahutaravidhaiḥ sannipātādasādhyā ||
children.translated_text: It slips from its proper place and again touches the finger; by many such conditions it is incurable because of <s>sannipāta</s> (the conjunction of all three doṣas).

children.text: pūrvaṃ pittagatiṃ prabhañjanagatiṃ śleṣmāṇam ābibhratīṃ svasthānabhramaṇaṃ muhurvidadhatīṃ cakrādhirūḍhāmiva
children.translated_text: First bearing the movement of pitta, then the movement of wind, then phlegm, repeatedly wandering from its own place as if mounted on a wheel,

children.text: tīvratvaṃ dadhatīṃ kalāpigatikāṃ sūkṣmatvamātanvatīṃ no sādhyāṃ dhamanīṃ vadanti munayo nāḍīgatijñāninaḥ ||
children.translated_text: assuming sharpness, having a peacock-like gait, and extending into subtlety: the sages who know pulse movement say that such an artery is not curable.
Just as a woodpecker strikes wood with very great speed,

children.text: sthitvā sthitvā calati yā sannipātena jāyate ||
children.translated_text: so the pulse that moves after stopping again and again is produced by <s>sannipāta</s>.
It trembles and throbs like a thread, and again touches the finger;
one should know that pulse to be incurable, and should avoid it from afar.
At the mouth the pulse may flow sharply, and at times it may flow cold;

children.text: āyāti picchilaḥ svedaḥ saptarātraṃ na jīvati ||
children.translated_text: sticky sweat comes on, and the patient does not live seven nights.

children.text: dehe śaityaṃ mukhe śvāso nāḍī tīvrātidāhikā
children.translated_text: There is coldness in the body, breath at the mouth, and a pulse that is sharp and exceedingly burning;
his life lasts half a month: so it is stated by the knower of the pulse.

children.text: mukhe nāḍī yadā nāsti madhye śaityaṃ bahiḥ klamaḥ
children.translated_text: When there is no pulse at the mouth, there is coldness in the middle, and exhaustion outwardly,

children.text: tantumandā vahennāḍī trirātraṃ na sa jīvati ||
children.translated_text: and the pulse flows threadlike and slow, he does not live three nights.

children.text: pūrvaṃ nāḍī tu vegotthā tataḥ paradine yadi
children.translated_text: If at first the pulse has arisen with force, but then on the following day
it becomes cold and deprived of force, then there is danger from <s>sannipāta</s>.
If on the preceding day the fever was extremely like fire,
and when the pulse moves continuously in a single lava of time,

children.text: mukhasthāne tu rugṇasya caturthe maraṇaṃ dine ||
children.translated_text: at the mouth-place of the sick man, death occurs on the fourth day.

children.text: mukhe truṭatyakasmācca na kiṃcid dṛśyate yadā
children.translated_text: When at the mouth it suddenly breaks off and nothing at all is perceived,

children.text: tadā vidyātsa rugṇānāṃ dvitīye maraṇaṃ dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: then one should know that for such sick people death on the second day is certain.

children.text: yadā nāḍī hatāvegā spandate naiva labhate
children.translated_text: When the pulse, its force struck down, throbs but does not regain itself,

children.text: tadā dinasya madhye tu maraṇaṃ rogiṇo bhavet ||
children.translated_text: then the patient's death occurs in the middle of the day.
When, at the mouth-place, the pulse whirls continuously like a ḍamaru drum,

children.text: calā nāḍī tu rugṇasya dinaikānmaraṇaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: that moving pulse of the sick man means death within one day.
When it is extremely subtle, separate, swift, forceful, full and moist,
appearing again and again and then dying away, then one should know incurability.

children.text: lakṣaṇe svasthasya talagā pūrvaṃ nāḍī syād aprapañcanāt ||
children.translated_text: As a sign in a healthy person, at first the pulse should be in the palm, without expansion.
When, through further expansion, it becomes subtle, the man dies within three days.
If, with the hand raised upward, it has the speed of lightning, the man dies within seven days.

children.text: śānte nāḍīvitāne śamanamupagate cendriyāṇāṃ pracāre sūkṣme vānuṣṇarūpāṃ vikṛtimupagate sarvathā śītabhāve
children.translated_text: When the network of pulses is quiet, when the activity of the senses has come to cessation, when it has become subtle, neither hot in form, altered, and altogether cold,

children.text: śūnye cittātmamārge sphuraṇavirahite naṣṭasaṃjñāpracāre sūrye candrātmasaṃsthe 'vagataguṇagaṇe pañcateyaṃ pravācyā ||
children.translated_text: when the path of mind and self is empty, devoid of throbbing, and the course of consciousness is lost, when sun and moon stand in the self and the aggregate of qualities has departed, this is to be called <s>pañcatva</s> (dissolution into the five elements).

children.text: nāḍyādiprakaraḥ prayāti vikṛtiṃ śāntiṃ parāṃ sūkṣmatāṃ kāntir yāti viparyayaṃ ca yadi vā hitvā svamārgānilam
children.translated_text: If the process beginning with the pulse goes into alteration, supreme quiet, and subtlety, and if the complexion becomes reversed after leaving its own path of wind,

children.text: ajñāne'pi hi śūnyatām upagate jñānendriye śāmyati sūryācandramasau tathā ca pihite pañcatvameti sphuṭam ||
children.translated_text: and if even without cognition it has gone to emptiness, the cognitive faculty grows still, and the sun and moon are likewise covered, then clearly the person reaches <s>pañcatva</s>.

children.text: śuṣkoṣṭhaḥ śyāvakoṣṭhe 'pyāsataradanakhaḥ śītanāsāpradeśaḥ śoṇākṣaścaikanetro lulitakarapadaḥ śrotrapātityayuktaḥ
children.translated_text: At the time of death a man becomes one whose lips are dry, whose belly is dark, whose palate, teeth, and nails are parched, whose nasal region is cold, whose eyes are red, whose one eye is affected, whose hands and feet are disordered, and who has falling of the ears;

children.text: śītaḥ śvāso'thavoṣṇaḥ śvasanasamudayī śītagātraḥ sakampaḥ sodvego niṣprapañcaḥ prabhavati manujaḥ sarvathā mṛtyukāle ||
children.translated_text: his breath is cold or hot, arising with labored respiration; his limbs are cold, he trembles, is agitated, and is without outward activity in every way.
Then, overcome by the five elements, five times over, they place the five senses among the five,
and having placed the five senses among the five, at the time of destruction they go to <s>pañcatva</s>.

children.text: vātāvartitamānuṣe 'tiviṣamaṃ saṃspandate nāḍikā pittasyaiva samāgamaṃ na kurute mandā ca mandodaye
children.translated_text: In a person turned about by vāta, the small pulse throbs in an exceedingly irregular way; it does not come into conjunction with pitta, and it is slow with a slow arising.

children.text: prācuryaṃ bhajate rasāśrayavaśātkṣīṇā rasenojjhitā nītvā śvāsamupaiti śāntimacalaiḥ khair antakāle nṛṇām ||
children.translated_text: It attains abundance through dependence on rasa, becomes diminished when abandoned by rasa, and, having carried the breath, comes to rest with the apertures unmoving at the time of people's death.
When the earth-pulse throbs with one measure thirty times,

children.text: svasthāne'pi tadā nūnaṃ rogī jīvati nānyathā ||
children.translated_text: then, even in its proper place, the sick person certainly lives, and not otherwise.

children.text: śarīraṃ śītalaṃ nāḍī nūnaṃ coṣṇatarā bhavet
children.translated_text: If the body is cold and the pulse is certainly rather hot,
the best physician should know that his fever is internal.
Having recognized the earth-pulse as facing death, one should not treat the patient afflicted by disease;
there one should have the medicine of <s>Rāma</s>'s name administered, for the sake of the next world.
